title: John Dewey
orientation: Russell treats John Dewey (b. 1859) as 'the leading living philosopher of America,' a man he admires personally and agrees with on most practical and political questions, but from whose central philosophical doctrine he dissents: Dewey's substitution of 'inquiry' for 'truth' as the fundamental concept of logic and the theory of knowledge (a position Dewey calls 'instrumentalism'). The chapter works through Russell's own rival account of truth and belief, a close critique of Dewey's definition of 'inquiry,' and closes with a broader warning about the 'cosmic impiety' Russell fears in any philosophy, Dewey's included, that treats truth as something human power can ultimately control.
historical_background: Like James, Dewey belongs to the New England liberal tradition. He became professor of philosophy at Chicago in 1894 (pedagogy among his subjects), founded a progressive school, and wrote The School and Society (1899), his most influential book on education. He was reluctantly a supporter of the First World War, took part in the inquiry into Trotsky's alleged guilt (concluding the charges were unfounded, though he doubted a Trotsky-led Soviet regime would have been satisfactory either), and, though very liberal economically, was never a Marxist.
philosophical_problems: Should 'truth' or 'inquiry' be taken as the fundamental concept of logic and epistemology?
Is truth static, final, and independent of human power (fixed by the past), or is it something that can be shaped by future action?
What distinguishes genuine 'inquiry' from any other process that reorganizes raw material into a 'unified whole' (e.g., a bricklayer's work)?
Should beliefs about the past be judged by their causes or by their future effects?
Is the confidence that truth can be brought under human control a healthy expression of modern power, or a dangerous 'intoxication of power'?

philosophers_discussed.name: John Dewey
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's primary subject. Russell praises his character and influence, agrees with much of his outlook, but subjects his instrumentalist theory of truth ('inquiry' and 'warranted assertability') to detailed, respectful criticism.

philosophers_discussed.name: William James
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as sharing Dewey's New England background and pragmatist orientation, but contrasted with him: James's pragmatism is 'concerned primarily with religion and morals,' while Dewey's is 'scientific,' derived from an examination of scientific method.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hegel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an early influence on Dewey's conception of knowledge as an organic, evolving whole; Russell argues Dewey's notion of inquiry producing 'unified wholes' still carries an unacknowledged Hegelian metaphysic of organism, even though Dewey rejects Hegel's Absolute and eternal world.

philosophers_discussed.name: C. S. Peirce
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted for his definition of truth, which Dewey approvingly cites: 'the opinion which is fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate.'

philosophers_discussed.name: George Raymond Geiger
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted as a laudatory supporter of Dewey who compared Dewey's method to a 'revolution in thought' as stupendous as the industrial revolution, cited by Russell to support his claim that Dewey's philosophy harmonizes with the age of industrialism.

philosophers_discussed.name: George Santayana
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted criticizing Dewey for a 'pervasive quasi-Hegelian tendency to dissolve the individual into his social functions,' corroborating Russell's own reading of Dewey.

philosophers_discussed.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Contrasted with Dewey: both are 'power philosophies,' but Nietzsche's is a philosophy of individual power, whereas Dewey's values the power of the community.

philosophers_discussed.name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the philosopher with whom the 'intoxication of power' first invaded philosophy, a danger Russell fears modern instrumentalism risks reviving.

philosophers_discussed.name: Giovanni Papini
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an Italian pragmatist who urged substituting the 'Imitation of God' for the 'Imitation of Christ,' offered as an extreme illustration of the modern collective sense of human power that concerns Russell.

schools_discussed: Hegelian idealism (as a residual influence on Dewey)

core_concepts.name: Instrumentalism: 'inquiry' in place of 'truth'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Dewey doesn't think of truth as a fixed, final thing waiting to be discovered, like an eternal fact. Instead he focuses on 'inquiry' -- the active process by which an organism (a person, a scientist) works to turn a confusing, unsettled situation into an orderly, resolved one.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Dewey's substitution of 'inquiry' for 'truth' as logic's fundamental concept; he defines inquiry as 'the controlled or directed transformation of an indeterminate situation into one that is so determinate in its constituent distinctions and relations as to convert the elements of the original situation into a unified whole,' concerned with 'objective transformations of objective subject-matter.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is, in Russell's words, 'his most distinctive philosophical doctrine,' rejecting the traditional view of truth as static, final, perfect and eternal (on the model of the multiplication table) in favor of a biological, evolutionary conception of thought.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed across Dewey's philosophical career; contrasted by Russell with the mathematics-linked notion of truth descending from Pythagoras and Plato.
examples: Reconnaissance before a battle, where a general adjusts his own forces to the enemy's dispositions, exemplifies 'inquiry' as mainly organism-side adjustment.
objections: Russell: Dewey's definition, taken literally, would also cover a drill-sergeant organizing recruits or a bricklayer arranging bricks, which Dewey would not call 'inquiry' -- so an unstated element is missing from the definition.

Russell: arranging a shuffled pack of cards into order and then treating that as 'the order resulting from inquiry' (rather than discovering the original order) only seems legitimate on an unacknowledged Hegelian assumption that reality is inherently orderly beneath a confused appearance.
competing_positions: The traditional view that inquiry is distinguished by its purpose of ascertaining truth -- a view unavailable to Dewey, who defines truth in terms of inquiry rather than the reverse
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell links the doctrine's flavor of active reshaping of the world to the industrial, technological confidence of the modern age.

core_concepts.name: Truth as caused by the past vs. 'warranted assertability' as determined by future effects
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell thinks a belief about something that already happened is true or false because of what actually happened -- fixed, unchangeable facts. Dewey instead judges beliefs 'good' or 'bad' (he avoids calling them simply true or false) by whether the actions they inspire turn out well in the future.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's view: a belief about a past occurrence is 'true,' or as nearly true as we can make it, in virtue of a certain relation to its causes, and since the past cannot be affected by present action, such truth is independent of present or future volition. Dewey's contrasting notion of 'warranted assertability' substitutes for 'truth' and depends on a belief's kind of effects, so that, in principle, altering the future could alter what is 'warrantedly assertable' about the past.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is presented by Russell as the fundamental divergence between his own outlook and Dewey's, with large implications for how much power human beings are thought to have over what counts as true.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed through Russell's own staircase and reconnaissance examples in direct engagement with Dewey's instrumentalism.
examples: A general's scouting reports are 'true,' on the common-sense/Russellian view, if the enemy really made the reported moves, regardless of whether the general later wins or loses the battle; Dewey's view instead classifies the reports 'satisfactory' or 'unsatisfactory' depending on the battle's outcome.

Whether one had coffee for breakfast: on Dewey's view, Russell argues, one would need to test the consequences of believing 'yes' against the consequences of believing 'no' before answering -- rather than simply trying to remember.

'Did Caesar cross the Rubicon?': Russell holds this unalterably fixed by the past event; on Dewey's account, in principle, a sufficiently skillful reshaping of the social environment could make the negative answer 'warrantedly assertable.'
objections: Russell finds this 'absurd': to know whether an ordinary claim is 'good' one would already need to know its consequences are 'good,' which in turn needs testing, and so on -- and different consequences may be judged good on different, competing grounds with no way to decide between them.
competing_positions: Dewey's 'warranted assertability,' judged by whether the activities a belief inspires have satisfactory or unsatisfactory consequences for the organism
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell connects the appeal of Dewey's view to 'the hopefulness engendered by machine production and the scientific manipulation of our physical environment.'

core_concepts.name: Organism and environment: belief as adjustment
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Rather than starting from 'minds' knowing 'objects,' Dewey (and, to an extent, Russell in his own sympathetic reconstruction) thinks of a living 'organism' interacting with its 'environment'; error is simply a failure of adjustment between the two, revealed for instance by the shock of surprise.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The framework, partly shared by Russell, that treats belief and error in terms of an organism's adjustment to its environment rather than a disembodied mind's grasp of facts; a false belief is (when testable) one that, in suitable circumstances, causes the believer surprise, while a true belief does not -- though Russell notes this test of surprise, while often useful, does not give the meaning of 'true' and 'false' and is not always applicable (e.g., one struck dead by lightning experiences no surprise despite having been mistaken).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the common ground from which Russell's and Dewey's accounts diverge, and shows how far Russell is willing to go toward Dewey's naturalistic, biological framing before parting ways over the definition of inquiry and truth.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Introduced by Russell via his own staircase example (misjudging when one has reached the bottom of a flight of stairs) before applying it to Dewey's theory.
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: Bertrand Russell (in dialogue with John Dewey)
examples: Misjudging the bottom step of a staircase and being jolted by the resulting shock of surprise.
The lion-escaped-at-the-zoo example: a sentence 'means' an event if it promotes the same behaviour the event itself would promote.

core_concepts.name: Cosmic impiety and the intoxication of power
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell worries that philosophies which make truth depend on human action, rather than on facts we cannot control, encourage a dangerous pride -- the feeling that humanity can remake reality itself to suit its wishes, with no limits imposed by 'stubborn facts.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis of a broader intellectual and political danger: the traditional concept of 'truth' as dependent on facts largely outside human control has historically instilled a necessary humility in philosophy; when instrumentalism removes this check, it takes 'a further step... on the road towards a certain kind of madness -- the intoxication of power which invaded philosophy with Fichte,' a danger Russell calls the greatest of his time.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is Russell's culminating criticism of instrumentalism, generalizing his technical objections into a warning about the social and political consequences of any philosophy of unlimited human power, whether individual (Nietzsche) or collective (Dewey).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Fichte as the point at which this 'intoxication' entered philosophy, and illustrated by the modern Italian pragmatist Papini's call to substitute the 'Imitation of God' for the 'Imitation of Christ.'
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: Bertrand Russell (as a critique of John Dewey and modern power-philosophies generally)
examples: The historical progression from Greek dread of hubris, through Christian humility before God, to Renaissance human pride, to modern technique's revival of 'the sense of the collective power of human communities.'
Papini's slogan urging the 'Imitation of God' in place of the 'Imitation of Christ.'
competing_positions: Dewey's own instrumentalism, which Russell treats not as consciously embracing this danger but as unintentionally contributing to it
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly framed by Russell in terms of humanity's changing religious and cultural relationship to a non-human universe, from Greek Necessity through Christian humility to modern technological pride.

arguments.title: Russell's critique of Dewey's definition of 'inquiry'
premises: Dewey defines inquiry as the controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate, unified whole through objective transformation of objective subject-matter.
A drill-sergeant organizing recruits, or a bricklayer arranging a heap of bricks, exactly fulfils this definition.
Dewey would not classify either activity as 'inquiry.'
arguments.conclusion: Dewey's definition of inquiry is incomplete: it omits an essential element that distinguishes genuine inquiry from mere organizing activity, an element Dewey never makes explicit.
arguments.explanation: Russell argues that traditionally this missing element would have been inquiry's purpose -- ascertaining truth -- but this option is closed to Dewey, since he defines truth in terms of inquiry rather than the other way around, leaving his account viciously incomplete or circular.
implications: Suggests that Dewey's notion of inquiry producing 'unified wholes' secretly relies on an unacknowledged Hegelian metaphysic in which reality is orderly beneath its confused appearances.

arguments.title: Russell's causal theory of truth versus Dewey's warranted assertability
premises: A belief about a past event either does or does not correspond to what actually happened; the past cannot now be altered by present or future action.
Dewey instead classifies beliefs as having 'warranted assertability' based on the future consequences of the activities they inspire.

To know whether a belief's consequences are 'good,' one must already judge that assessment true -- but on Dewey's own view, that judgement is itself only 'true' (warranted) if it too has good consequences.
arguments.conclusion: Dewey's account generates an infinite regress and reverses the natural order of explanation, judging beliefs by effects that themselves require prior judgements of truth to assess.
arguments.explanation: Russell's coffee-for-breakfast and Rubicon examples are designed to show the absurd practical consequences of always judging past-tense beliefs by future effects rather than by what actually happened.
implications: If sound, this shows warranted assertability cannot, after all, simply replace the ordinary, causally grounded notion of truth for beliefs about the past.

arguments.title: Russell's argument connecting instrumentalism to industrial power and 'cosmic impiety'
premises: Throughout the book, philosophies have tended to reflect the social environment of the philosophers who hold them.

The belief that human power can determine truth (rather than truth being fixed by 'stubborn facts' outside human control) is historically associated with the confidence generated by machine production and the scientific manipulation of the physical environment.
The traditional concept of truth as dependent on facts outside human control has functioned historically as a check on human pride (hubris).
arguments.conclusion: Instrumentalism, by weakening this check, risks contributing -- however unintentionally -- to a dangerous 'intoxication of power,' a form of cosmic impiety that Russell regards as the greatest danger of his time.
arguments.explanation: Russell draws an explicit historical arc from Greek fear of hubris, through Christian humility, to Renaissance pride and modern technological confidence, situating Dewey's instrumentalism (a philosophy of communal, not individual, power) within this arc alongside Nietzsche's philosophy of individual power.
objections: Dewey himself objected to Russell's earlier, similar claim linking pragmatism to American industrialism, comparing it to linking Russell's own philosophy to the interests of the English landed aristocracy; Russell accepts the criticism could apply to himself too but maintains he is not alone in making the connection, citing Santayana's similar remark about Dewey's 'quasi-Hegelian tendency to dissolve the individual into his social functions.'
implications: Generalizes Russell's technical objections to Dewey's theory of truth into a broader warning about any philosophy, individualist or collectivist, that removes humility toward a non-human reality.

key_distinctions: Truth as static, final, and independent of human power vs. inquiry as an ongoing, evolutionary, organism-environment process
Ascertaining truth vs. Dewey's 'inquiry' as transformation of an indeterminate into a determinate, unified situation
Truth judged by causes (what actually happened) vs. 'warranted assertability' judged by future effects
Power philosophy of the individual (Nietzsche) vs. power philosophy of the community (Dewey)
Humility before facts outside human control vs. the 'intoxication of power' that treats truth as humanly malleable
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces Dewey's conception of knowledge as an evolving, organic whole to the lingering influence of Hegel (despite Dewey's rejection of Hegel's Absolute and eternal Idea), and frames the traditional 'static, final' notion of truth Dewey rejects as descending from Pythagoras and Plato's linkage of mathematics and theology. He also situates the danger of instrumentalism's power philosophy as a modern descendant of the 'intoxication of power' he says first invaded philosophy with Fichte.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The chapter closes the book's discussion of American pragmatism (James, Schiller, Dewey) and sets up the final chapter's discussion of logical analysis, where Russell's own, technically developed alternative account of knowledge, truth, and the mind-matter relation is presented as the constructive counterpart to his critiques of Bergson, James, and Dewey.
political_social_context: Russell explicitly connects Dewey's instrumentalism to 'the age of industrialism and collective enterprise,' noting its especially strong appeal to Americans and to progressive elements in countries like China and Mexico; he recounts Dewey's own objection to this framing and Santayana's independent, corroborating criticism.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter's closing pages trace a long historical arc in humanity's religious and cultural stance toward the non-human universe -- Greek dread of hubris, Christian humility before God, Renaissance pride, and modern technological confidence -- culminating in Russell's warning about 'cosmic impiety' as a danger to which modern philosophy, including instrumentalism, may unintentionally contribute.
russell_presentation: Russell is unusually personal and warm toward Dewey, praising his character, his influence on education (paralleling Russell's own efforts), and his political good sense (opposition to Marxism and to violent revolution, informed by visits to Russia and China). He nonetheless dissents sharply from Dewey's core doctrine, walking through his own theory of truth and belief (via the staircase and lion-at-the-zoo examples) before turning to a close, largely destructive analysis of Dewey's official definition of 'inquiry,' which Russell argues is incomplete because it cannot, without circularity, distinguish inquiry from any other reorganizing activity. He then contrasts his own causally grounded notion of truth with Dewey's future-oriented 'warranted assertability,' using the general's battle reports, the coffee-for-breakfast example, and the Rubicon example to argue Dewey's view collapses into absurdity. The chapter (continuing without a section break into material that precedes the next chapter's heading) ends on Russell's broadest and most explicitly value-laden note in the book: a warning that any philosophy which erodes the check that 'stubborn facts' place on human pride edges toward what he calls 'cosmic impiety' and 'the intoxication of power,' which he names the greatest danger of his time.
critical_context: Common scholarly assessment: Dewey's defenders have argued that Russell's critique somewhat flattens 'warranted assertability' by treating it as a simple effects-based redefinition of 'true,' when Dewey intended it more narrowly as an account of justified assertion within ongoing scientific inquiry rather than a metaphysical claim that the past itself becomes alterable; Russell's 'coffee for breakfast' and Rubinox-style reductios are widely cited as rhetorically effective but are also sometimes judged, even by sympathetic readers, to caricature the more modest epistemological point Dewey was making about the fallibility and revisability of belief.
key_takeaways: Russell admires Dewey personally and agrees with much of his political and educational outlook, but dissents from Dewey's central doctrine: substituting 'inquiry' for 'truth.'

Dewey defines inquiry as transforming an indeterminate situation into a determinate, unified whole; Russell objects this definition, taken literally, would also cover a drill-sergeant's or bricklayer's work, and secretly depends on an unacknowledged Hegelian metaphysic.
Russell holds a belief about the past is true or false because of its causes (what actually happened); Dewey substitutes 'warranted assertability,' judged by a belief's future effects.
Russell argues Dewey's effects-based view produces an infinite regress and absurd results (illustrated by the coffee-for-breakfast and Rubicon examples).

The chapter closes with Russell's broader warning against 'cosmic impiety': philosophies (individualist, like Nietzsche's, or collectivist, like Dewey's) that erode humility before facts outside human control risk feeding a dangerous 'intoxication of power' traced back to Fichte.
study_notes:
Read this chapter as a model of Russell's method at its most personally generous and philosophically uncompromising at once: notice how carefully he separates his admiration for Dewey the man and the political thinker from his rejection of Dewey the epistemologist, explicitly refusing to let the first soften the second. 

The technical core is the drill-sergeant/bricklayer counterexample: try restating Dewey's official definition of 'inquiry' in your own words, then ask what a drill-sergeant organizing recruits and Dewey's scientist conducting inquiry could possibly have in common structurally -- both take a disorganized situation and make it determinate and unified. Russell's point is that Dewey needs some further ingredient (traditionally, the aim of finding out the truth) to mark inquiry off from mere reorganizing, but that Dewey has closed off the traditional answer by making truth depend on inquiry rather than the reverse.

The second technical core is the contrast between judging a belief by its causes (Russell) and by its effects (Dewey's 'warranted assertability'). Work through the Rubicon example carefully: Russell isn't just saying Dewey is impractical, he's arguing that on Dewey's view, since the future is in principle alterable by human power, so in principle is what counts as 'warrantedly assertable' about the past -- a conclusion Russell finds not just false but dangerous. This is what connects the technical epistemology to the chapter's closing meditation on hubris, humility, and the 'intoxication of power': for Russell, an epistemology that lets human will reach backward into the fixity of the past is one symptom of a larger and, in his view, historically dangerous inflation of human power.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Dewey's version of pragmatism, which treats beliefs and theories as tools for successfully handling situations rather than as fixed pictures of an unchanging truth.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Dewey's doctrine substituting 'inquiry' -- the controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate, unified one -- for 'truth' as logic's fundamental concept.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The active process of turning a confusing, unsettled situation into a clear, organized one.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Defined by Dewey as 'the controlled or directed transformation of an indeterminate situation into one that is so determinate in its constituent distinctions and relations as to convert the elements of the original situation into a unified whole.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Dewey's substitute for 'truth': a belief is justified to assert not because it matches a fixed fact, but because of how well the activities it inspires turn out.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Dewey's term, used in place of 'truth,' for the status a belief acquires when the activities it inspires in an organism have satisfactory rather than unsatisfactory consequences; contrasted by Russell with a causally grounded notion of truth about the past.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Russell's term for the dangerous pride of believing human beings can reshape reality (including truth itself) entirely to their own will, with no facts left to humble them.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's diagnosis of a modern philosophical and cultural danger arising when the traditional check of 'stubborn facts' (truth as independent of human power) is removed, tracing the danger's philosophical origin to Fichte and its cultural expression to modern technological confidence.

questions.prompt: What is Dewey's 'most distinctive philosophical doctrine,' according to Russell, and why does Russell say he must dissent from it despite his admiration for Dewey?
questions.answer: The substitution of 'inquiry' for 'truth' as the fundamental concept of logic and the theory of knowledge. Russell says that although he agrees with Dewey on most matters and admires him personally, he cannot accept this doctrine because he believes it leads to an incomplete or circular account of inquiry and an untenable, effects-based account of truth about the past.
questions.explanation: Russell states this dissent explicitly at the chapter's opening, framing the personal-versus-philosophical tension that runs through the chapter.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's drill-sergeant/bricklayer objection to Dewey's definition of 'inquiry.'
questions.answer: Dewey defines inquiry as the controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate, unified whole through objective transformation of objective subject-matter. A drill-sergeant organizing raw recruits, or a bricklayer arranging a heap of bricks, exactly satisfies this definition, yet Dewey would not call either activity 'inquiry.' Therefore Dewey's definition omits some further, unstated element -- traditionally, the aim of ascertaining truth -- that distinguishes genuine inquiry from mere reorganizing activity; but this traditional answer is unavailable to Dewey since he defines truth in terms of inquiry, not the reverse.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's central technical criticism of Dewey's official definition of inquiry.

questions.prompt: Compare Russell's and Dewey's accounts of what makes a belief about a past event 'true.'
questions.answer: Russell holds a belief about the past is true (or as nearly true as possible) in virtue of a relation to its causes -- what actually happened -- and since the past cannot be affected by present or future action, such truth is fixed and independent of human will. Dewey substitutes 'warranted assertability,' judged by whether the activities a belief inspires have satisfactory or unsatisfactory future consequences, so that, in principle, altering the future could alter what is warrantedly assertable about the past.
questions.explanation: Russell illustrates this with the example of whether Caesar crossed the Rubicon and with a general's battle reports.

questions.prompt: What example does Russell use to satirize the practical consequences of judging ordinary beliefs by their future effects rather than their causes?
questions.answer: The example of being asked whether one had coffee with breakfast: on Dewey's view, Russell suggests, one would have to test the consequences of believing 'yes' against the consequences of believing 'no,' compare which is more satisfactory, and only then decide -- rather than simply trying to remember.
questions.explanation: Russell calls the resulting procedure absurd, since even judging the consequences 'good' would itself require another such test, ad infinitum.

questions.prompt: What is 'cosmic impiety,' and to which earlier philosopher does Russell trace its origin in modern philosophy?
questions.answer: Cosmic impiety is Russell's term for the dangerous pride that arises when human beings lose the humility instilled by the traditional idea that truth depends on facts outside human control, believing instead that even truth can be reshaped by human power. Russell traces the 'intoxication of power' underlying it to Fichte.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's closing warning, connecting his critique of Dewey's instrumentalism to a broader cultural and political concern.

questions.prompt: How does Russell compare Dewey's 'power philosophy' to Nietzsche's?
questions.answer: Both are power philosophies, but Nietzsche's is a philosophy of individual power, whereas Dewey's values the power of the community -- it is the collective, social power of human communities, not any single person's will, that Dewey's instrumentalism treats as valuable.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this comparison to situate Dewey within a broader pattern of modern 'power philosophies' he finds worrying.

questions.prompt: How did Dewey respond to Russell's earlier claim linking pragmatism to 'obnoxious aspects of American industrialism,' and how does Russell answer him?
questions.answer: Dewey objected that this was much as if he linked Russell's own philosophy to the interests of the English landed aristocracy. Russell replies that he is used to having his views explained by his aristocratic background, is willing to accept his own views are shaped by social environment, and regrets the mistake if he was wrong about Dewey -- but notes Santayana independently made a similar criticism of Dewey's tendency to dissolve the individual into social functions.
questions.explanation: This exchange shows Russell's characteristic even-handedness even while defending his interpretive claim.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, Dewey's notion that inquiry produces 'unified wholes' secretly depends on an unacknowledged influence from which earlier philosopher?
quiz.explanation: Russell argues that without a Hegelian distinction between a confused appearance and an orderly, organic reality, there is no reason inquiry should be expected to yield 'unified wholes.'

quiz.prompt: Russell traces the philosophical origin of the 'intoxication of power' to ____.
quiz.explanation: Russell states this intoxication of power 'invaded philosophy with Fichte.'
quiz.related_concept: Cosmic impiety and the intoxication of power

quiz.prompt: How does Russell distinguish Dewey's 'power philosophy' from Nietzsche's?
options: Dewey's is religious, Nietzsche's is secular
Dewey's values the power of the community; Nietzsche's values individual power
Dewey rejects all forms of power; Nietzsche embraces them
There is no difference between them
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly draws this contrast in the chapter's closing pages.
quiz.related_concept: Cosmic impiety and the intoxication of power

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's drill-sergeant/bricklayer objection to Dewey's definition of 'inquiry.' Does the missing element Russell identifies (the aim of ascertaining truth) genuinely distinguish inquiry from other organizing activities, or could a defender of Dewey supply a different missing element that avoids Russell's circularity charge?
rubric: Accurately states Dewey's definition and Russell's counterexample
Explains the circularity problem Russell identifies

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Russell's causally grounded theory of truth with Dewey's 'warranted assertability.' Using the Rubicon or coffee-for-breakfast example, explain which account better fits ordinary practices of investigating the past.
rubric: Identifies the key point of disagreement (causes vs. effects)

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Russell's concept of 'cosmic impiety.' Is Russell's argument that instrumentalism risks feeding an 'intoxication of power' a fair extension of his technical criticism of Dewey's theory of truth, or an overreach connecting a narrow epistemological disagreement to a much larger political and cultural claim?
rubric: Explains 'cosmic impiety' and its historical framing accurately
Traces the argument's connection to the technical critique of warranted assertability
Considers whether the extension is justified
